clause_b.excerpt: The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF) Guide … Saudi Central Bank

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_record_keepin.implication: Record management systems — including third-party outsourced archives — must contractually preserve SAMA's right of direct access to AML/CTF records; the institution must be able to retrieve and produce any record on demand, with periodic tests (at least annually) evidencing system effectiveness.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_record_keepin.why: The Wire Transfer section explicitly cross-references the Record Keeping section as the governing retention standard for beneficiary identity verification data collected during wire transfers, and record keeping para 6.8 specifically addresses wire transfer record obligations, creating a direct normative cross-reference between the two regimes.

clause_a.excerpt: 6.8 When conducting wire trans[fers] … [record keeping obligations apply]

clause_b.excerpt: the financial institution receiving a wire transfer shall verify the beneficiary's identity and keep this information as stated under the Record Keeping Section.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_record_keepin.implication: Wire transfer processing systems must retain originator and beneficiary data fields (name, account/reference number, address/ID, purpose, relationship) for a minimum of ten years in a retrievable and auditable format, with records available to SAMA and competent authorities upon request — this data retention requirement must be built into the payment messaging and archiving infrastructure.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_correspondent.why: Section 13 of the Correspondence Relationship regime explicitly cross-references the Monitoring of Transactions and Activities Section, requiring financial institutions to apply continuous control measures from that section specifically to detect unusual activity in correspondent accounts, making transaction monitoring an embedded obligation within correspondent banking due diligence.

clause_a.excerpt: The financial institution should apply appropriate control measures as indicated under the Monitoring of Transactions and Activities Section, including continuous control measures for correspondence accounts to detect any unusual activity or behavior in the correspondence relati…

clause_b.excerpt: The financial institution shall put in place measures and procedures based on the risk assessment results to monitor transactions and identify unusual transactions and activities. The measures and procedures shall be effectively implemented and documented by the financial instit…

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_correspondent.implication: Correspondent account monitoring must be configured as a distinct, continuously active rule set within the transaction monitoring system, with documented senior-management approval, evidencing that general monitoring obligations under Section 7 are applied at the correspondent-relationship level.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_monitoring_tr.why: Section 7 explicitly identifies detection and referral of suspicious transactions to the SAFIU as the primary output of transaction monitoring, establishing a direct procedural dependency: the monitoring function triggers the reporting obligation defined in Section 8, creating an end-to-end detect-to-report workflow.

clause_a.excerpt: The monitoring of transactions and activities, including those unusual and suspicious, is an important element for applying the risk-based approach as it enables the financial institution to identify and report any suspicious transactions or activities to the SAFIU.

clause_b.excerpt: The financial institution shall immediately and directly inform the SAFIU upon suspicion or the presence of information or reasonable grounds to suspect that a customer's behavior is related to ML/TF acts.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_monitoring_tr.implication: The transaction monitoring system must have a documented escalation path that converts flagged unusual activity into a timed STR workflow, with evidence of investigation, approval levels, and SAFIU submission timestamps auditable end-to-end.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_amlctf_compli.why: Section 9 assigns the AML/CTF Compliance Function officer direct operational responsibility for receiving, analysing, and escalating suspicious transaction reports to the SAFIU, expressly cross-referencing the Reporting of Suspicious Transactions Section as the governing procedure, making the compliance function the accountable owner of the STR lifecycle.

clause_a.excerpt: Reporting suspicious transactions to the SAFIU as soon as the suspicion is detected in accordance with the reporting procedures followed in addition to preparing a technical report on the suspicion case as stated in the Reporting of Suspicious Transactions Section.

clause_b.excerpt: The financial institution shall set up and document procedures for reporting suspicious transactions, implementing them effectively, and ensuring that they are approved at the level of the board of directors.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_amlctf_compli.implication: The AML/CTF compliance officer must be named in board-approved STR procedures as the accountable decision-maker for SAFIU submissions, and the system must capture a dated audit trail from internal flag through officer review to SAFIU dispatch.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_reporting_sus.why: The Reporting of Suspicious Transactions section mandates direct reporting to SAMA (alongside SAFIU) for accounts and transactions linked to UN Security Council designation lists, and requires submission of internal controls surveys and AML/CTF data to SAMA, establishing SAMA as a parallel regulatory recipient distinct from the SAFIU intelligence function.

clause_a.excerpt: Reporting any accounts, business relationships, or financial transactions related to the names included in the lists of the Security Council committees… to SAMA, as mentioned in Paragraph (8.15) under the Reporting of Suspicious Transactions Section.

clause_b.excerpt: The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF) Guide — AML/CTF Department, Saudi Central Bank, RABI' I 1441H (November 2019).

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_reporting_sus.implication: Compliance systems must maintain two distinct reporting channels — SAFIU for STRs and SAMA for sanctions-linked account notifications — with separate workflow triggers, submission records, and response tracking for each regulator.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_amlctf_compli.why: Both the AML/CTF Compliance Function (Section 9) and the Independent Audit Function (Section 10) are mandated governance layers under the same AML/CTF program, with the compliance function explicitly responsible for the program that the independent auditor must test for effectiveness, creating a principal-reviewer relationship between the two nodes.

clause_a.excerpt: The financial institution shall establish an independent and specialized AML/CTF unit and provide it with sufficient resources, including human and technological resources, to carry out its work perfectly.

clause_b.excerpt: The financial institution shall have the AML/CTF internal controls tested by an independent party to ensure that they are adequate to ML/TF risks and implemented effectively… the internal or external auditors involved shall have sufficient experience to conduct a risk-based test…

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_amlctf_compli.implication: The independent auditor's scope must be formally documented to cover the compliance function's program, with findings tracked to management responses, and the auditor must be structurally segregated from the AML/CTF unit to satisfy Para 10.2's independence requirement — evidenced in audit-charter and organisational-chart documentation.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_amlctf_traini.why: The AML/CTF Training obligations derive directly from SAMA's AML/CTF Guide issued by the Saudi Central Bank, and the senior management training mandate is framed as a SAMA-supervised requirement under the implementing regulations of both the Anti-Money Laundering Law and the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing, making SAMA the supervising authority against which training adequacy is measured.

clause_a.excerpt: Providing appropriate specialized training for employees in the AML/CTF compliance department and those working in the same field on an annual basis to ensure effective performance of their duties and functions.

clause_b.excerpt: The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF) Guide — AML/CTF Department, Saudi Central Bank, RABI' I 1441H (November 2019).

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_amlctf_traini.implication: Financial institutions must maintain annually updated training records — including attendance logs, curriculum content, and competency assessments — that SAMA examiners can request to verify compliance with the at-minimum-annual training cadence specified for AML/CTF staff.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_recruitment_c.why: SAMA's AML/CTF Guide explicitly lists 'Recruitment and Follow-up Criteria' as a mandatory element of the AML/CTF program that financial institutions must adopt, making it a named sub-section within the SAMA-issued guide and thus directly referencing the issuing authority's regulatory framework.

clause_a.excerpt: The financial institution shall include, as a minimum, the following elements in its internal policy and procedures for combating ML/TF: ... h) Recruitment and follow-up criteria.

clause_b.excerpt: 12. Recruitment and Following-up Criteria ... The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF) Guide ... Saudi Central Bank RABI' I 1441H (November 2019)

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_recruitment_c.implication: A SAMA examiner will expect a financial institution's AML/CTF program documentation to include a standalone, board-approved policy section on recruitment and follow-up criteria, evidencing that staff integrity checks are embedded as a minimum program element rather than an informal HR practice.

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_sama||markdow.why: SAMA's AML/CTF Guide incorporates Wire Transfer as a numbered section (Section 14) within the guide itself, establishing mandatory originator/beneficiary information requirements and processing obligations that financial institutions in Saudi Arabia must implement under SAMA's supervisory authority.

clause_b.excerpt: Article (10) of the Anti-Money Laundering Law and Article (68) of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing state the obligations of the financial institution when conducting cross-border and domestic wire transfers in any currency.

clause_a.excerpt: 14. Wire Transfer ... The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF) Guide ... AML/CTF Department, Saudi Central Bank

markdown_sama_en_1704_ver1_sama||markdow.implication: Financial institutions must configure wire transfer processing systems to capture and transmit, at minimum, originator full name, account/reference number, address/ID, beneficiary full name, beneficiary account/reference, and transfer purpose — with automated detection of missing fields and a documented risk-based decision workflow for executing, rejecting, or suspending incomplete transfers.

markdown_sama_en_2082_ver1_debt_purchase.why: The Consumer Finance Debt Purchase Instructions (Article 8) mandate that the purchasing finance company must use SARIE (the Saudi Fast Transfer System) as the exclusive settlement channel for repaying outstanding debts, and prescribe a minimum data set that each SARIE payment message must carry, directly linking the debt-purchase process to the SARIE system as a required operational control.

clause_a.excerpt: على شركة التمويل الراغبة في شراء المديونية استخدام النظام السعودي للتحويلات المالية السريعة "سريع" لسداد المديونيات القائمة. ويجب أن تتضمن دفعة السداد الصادرة عبر نظام "سريع" بحد أدنى البيانات الآتية: اسم العميل، رقم الهوية الوطنية/ الإقامة، مبلغ المديونية، الغرض من التحويل، رقم…

clause_b.excerpt: استخدام النظام السعودي للتحويلات المالية السريعة "سريع" لسداد المديونيات القائمة

markdown_sama_en_2082_ver1_debt_purchase.implication: The purchasing finance company's operational system must enforce SARIE as the sole settlement rail for debt-purchase payments and validate that each outgoing SARIE message includes all five mandatory data fields (customer name, national/residence ID, debt amount, transfer purpose, debt reference number) before submission — creating an auditable, structured payment record linking the transaction to the specific consumer debt being extinguished.
markdown_sama_en_2082_ver1_debt_purchase.caveat: Both clause_a and clause_b are drawn from the same Article 8 source paragraph; the node_b context for SARIE does not contain a distinct standalone definition excerpt, so both excerpts reference the operative obligation text. OCR/bidi rendering of the Arabic source may affect exact field-name rendering.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_detect||markd.why: The Detect Domain is one of the four mandated domains within the Counter-Fraud Framework structure; the Framework explicitly names Detect as a required domain and prescribes that each domain's Principles and Control Requirements must be implemented by Member Organisations.

clause_a.excerpt: Fraud detection systems and controls are risk-based measures to identify fraud by looking for indicators in customer behaviours, transactional and non-transactional information.

clause_b.excerpt: The Framework is structured around four main domains, namely: Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond. For each domain, several sub-domains are defined.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_detect||markd.implication: A SAMA examiner will expect Member Organisations to evidence that fraud detection standards (covering data sources, system calibration, roles, and thresholds) are formally documented as part of the overarching Counter-Fraud Framework, with maturity-model scoring applied to each Detect sub-domain.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.why: The Governance Domain is the first and foundational domain of the Counter-Fraud Framework; the Framework explicitly positions Board and Executive Leadership accountability, the Counter-Fraud Governance Committee (CFGC), and the Counter-Fraud Programme as prerequisite structural requirements that enable all other domains.

clause_a.excerpt: The Framework is structured around four main domains, namely: Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond… The Control Requirements reflect the mandated Counter-Fraud controls that should be considered by Member Organisations when designing and implementing a Counter-Fraud Programme.

clause_b.excerpt: The Board and Executive Leadership of the Member Organisation is ultimately responsible for creation of a Counter-Fraud Programme; providing leadership and direction; and projecting a Counter-Fraud culture inside and outside the organisation.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.implication: Compliance officers must ensure that CFGC establishment, Board endorsement of the Counter-Fraud Strategy/Policy/Risk Appetite, and appointment of a Head of Counter-Fraud are evidenced before the organisation can claim any maturity level above 0 in any Framework domain.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.why: The Counter-Fraud Framework mandates measurement of Member Organisations' control implementation via the Counter-Fraud Maturity Model, making the model the primary assessment instrument embedded within and referenced by the Framework. Achieving higher maturity levels (3–5) is a sequential, criteria-gated progression that governs how the Framework's control requirements are evidenced and benchmarked.

clause_a.excerpt: The Counter-Fraud maturity level will be measured with the help of a predefined maturity model. The Counter-Fraud Maturity Model distinguishes 6 maturity levels (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5).

clause_b.excerpt: To achieve maturity level 4, Member Organisations should periodically measure and evaluate the effectiveness of the Counter-Fraud controls implemented to achieve maturity level 3... Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) should be defined.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.implication: A SAMA examiner will expect Member Organisations to maintain documented, time-stamped maturity assessments mapped to specific control requirements, with evidence trails showing sequential fulfilment of criteria for each level (0–5) including KPI/KRI records for levels 4 and 5.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.why: The Counter-Fraud Framework explicitly designates 'Prevent' as one of its four structural domains, with the Framework's control requirement numbering system, governance obligations, and Fraud Risk Assessment outputs all feeding directly into the Prevent domain's standards, thresholds, and control design obligations.

clause_a.excerpt: The Framework is structured around four main domains, namely: Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond. For each domain, several sub-domains are defined... the Framework states a Principle and related Control Requirements.

clause_b.excerpt: An effective Counter-Fraud Programme includes fraud prevention processes and controls to facilitate the identification of threats and mitigate the risk of fraud occurring... The Fraud Risk Management Framework should be defined, approved and implemented.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.implication: Compliance teams must map each Prevent-domain control requirement (e.g., authentication, transaction limits, due diligence) back to the Fraud Risk Assessment output and Fraud Risk Appetite thresholds, with documented rationale that prevention controls are proportionate—an auditor will check this linkage explicitly.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.why: The Counter-Fraud Framework designates 'Respond' as the fourth structural domain and requires the Head of Counter-Fraud to develop systems to 'prevent, detect and respond to fraud', making the Fraud Response Plan an obligatory component of the Framework's overall programme architecture.

clause_a.excerpt: Developing a risk-based Counter-Fraud Programme that addresses people, process, and technology, including adequate systems to prevent, detect and respond to fraud.

clause_b.excerpt: A timely and effective response to incidents of actual or suspected fraud is key to minimising losses... Member Organisations should define, approve, implement and maintain a Fraud Response Plan to outline the organisational response to an actual or suspected fraud incident.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.implication: The Fraud Response Plan must be formally approved, aligned with enterprise incident management, and its compliance monitored, meaning RegTech systems should capture case timestamps, escalation decisions, and resolution outcomes to evidence prompt and competent response as required by the Framework.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.why: The Counter-Fraud Framework is issued by SAMA and imposes obligations on Member Organisations, with SAMA retaining supervisory roles including receiving intelligence, notifications of new fraud typologies, and overseeing compliance via maturity assessments. The document's authority flows directly from SAMA's regulatory mandate.

clause_a.excerpt: Sharing Counter-Fraud Intelligence with SAMA and other organisations in the sector.

clause_b.excerpt: Counter-Fraud Framework, Saudi Central Bank, October 2022, Version 1.0

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.implication: Member Organisations must build a structured channel (e.g., supervisory notification workflow) to transmit fraud intelligence and new typology alerts to SAMA, evidencing this as a documented, recurring process subject to examiner review.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.why: The Preauthorization/Notification POS Fraud Circular explicitly cross-references the Counter-Fraud Framework (issued under SAMA circular No. 501011), requiring acquiring service providers to comply with it; the Framework thus sets the minimum control standards that the circular operationalises for preauthorization fraud scenarios.

clause_a.excerpt: Proactively and reactively tuning Counter-Fraud systems... developing Fraud Monitoring & Detection System capabilities.

clause_b.excerpt: مع التأكيد على الالتزام التام بدليل مكافحة الاحتيال المالي المبلغ بموجب تعميم البنك المركزي رقم ٥٠١٠١١ [with full commitment to the Counter-Fraud Guide issued under SAMA circular No. 501011]

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.implication: Acquiring service providers must map their preauthorization transaction monitoring and detection controls explicitly to the Counter-Fraud Framework's maturity requirements, and document this linkage to demonstrate compliance with both instruments to SAMA examiners.
markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_framework||ma.caveat: The Arabic circular references circular No. 501011 as the Counter-Fraud Guide; confirmation that SAMA_EN_2217_VER1 corresponds to that circular number relies on contextual inference rather than an explicit identifier visible in the English document.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_cfgc||markdow.why: The CFGC is a mandatory structural element of the Governance domain: the Governance sub-domain 3.1 requires Member Organisations to establish and maintain the CFGC, and the CFGC is the formal approval and oversight body for all key governance artefacts (strategy, policy, fraud risk appetite) described throughout Section 3.

clause_a.excerpt: Approving the CFGC charter... Endorsing (after being approved by the CFGC): the Counter-Fraud Strategy... Counter-Fraud Policy... output of the Fraud Risk Assessment... Fraud Risk Appetite.

clause_b.excerpt: Member Organisations should establish and maintain a dedicated Counter-Fraud Governance Committee (CFGC)... headed by a member of the Executive Committee (e.g., CEO, CRO or equivalent).

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_cfgc||markdow.implication: Examiners will expect to see a formally constituted CFGC with a board-endorsed charter, documented membership at executive level, and evidence of CFGC approval for each of the five endorsed artefacts (strategy, policy, FRA output, risk appetite, roles); absence of any one constitutes a Governance domain control gap.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_authenticatio.why: The Authentication Standard is explicitly enumerated as a required system/technology control within the Prevent Domain's fraud prevention standards, making it a named sub-component of the broader prevention control architecture rather than a merely co-occurring concept.

clause_a.excerpt: Member Organisations should define, approve, implement and maintain a standard for the authentication of customer, employee and third party credentials and instructions to ensure information is protected and unauthorised access or actions are prevented.

clause_b.excerpt: Systems and technology implemented to prevent fraud (e.g., identity and access management, authentication, issuance of one-time-passwords, biometrics).

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_authenticatio.implication: A SAMA examiner will expect the Authentication Standard to be documented, cross-referenced within the fraud prevention standards policy, and subject to periodic review aligned to the Fraud Risk Assessment — authentication controls must appear in both the cyber-security and counter-fraud control inventories.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_due_diligence.why: Due Diligence Standards are explicitly listed as a mandated control category within the Prevent Domain's fraud prevention standards, serving as the primary mechanism for preventing establishment of fraudulent relationships with employees, customers and third parties before harm occurs.

clause_a.excerpt: Member Organisations should define, approve and implement standards for assessing the fraud risk associated with employees, customers and third parties to prevent the establishment of relationships outside risk appetite and manage fraud risks throughout the duration of the relat…

clause_b.excerpt: The controls implemented to prevent fraud (e.g., segregation of duties, approval and escalations, employee training, access restrictions, due diligence and integrity checks, notification of account changes, transaction limits, underwriting checks).

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_due_diligence.implication: Due Diligence Standards must be versioned artefacts that are explicitly cross-referenced in the fraud prevention standards document, with evidence of periodic review, risk-based tiering for employees/customers/third parties, and outcomes fed back into the Fraud Risk Assessment cycle.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_risk_as.why: The Fraud Risk Assessment is the primary input that determines the focus, proportionality, limits and thresholds of all controls within the Prevent Domain, creating a mandatory feed from assessment outputs into prevention standard design and update cycles.

clause_a.excerpt: Member Organisations should conduct a Fraud Risk Assessment to identify fraud risks to which they or their customers are subject and assess the effectiveness of controls in place to mitigate the risks.

clause_b.excerpt: The output of the Fraud Risk Assessment should be used to determine where prevention activity is focused, and controls should be proportionate to the risk appetite of the organisation.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_risk_as.implication: RegTech workflow must ensure that each refresh of the Fraud Risk Assessment triggers a documented review of fraud prevention standards, limits and thresholds, with a traceable audit trail linking residual risk ratings to specific preventive control updates or accepted risk decisions.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_intelligence_.why: Intelligence Monitoring is explicitly listed as a mandatory component of the Fraud Risk Management Framework within the Prevent domain; the Framework requires it to be addressed at a minimum alongside Fraud Risk Assessment, Fraud Risk Appetite, and KRIs, making it a structural sub-domain of Prevent.

clause_a.excerpt: The fraud Intelligence Monitoring process should be defined, approved, and implemented. [...] The Intelligence Monitoring process should include: Scanning, collation, analysis, assessment and dissemination of information on existing and emerging threats.

clause_b.excerpt: The Fraud Risk Management Framework should address at a minimum: 1. Intelligence Monitoring. 2. Fraud Risk Assessment. 3. Fraud Risk Appetite. 4. Key Risk Indicators (KRIs).

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_intelligence_.implication: Auditors should expect a documented, Board-approved Fraud Risk Management Framework that explicitly maps Intelligence Monitoring as a named sub-process with defined sources, dissemination paths (including to SAMA), and a periodic effectiveness evaluation cadence.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_prevent||mark.why: The Prevent domain's control requirements mandate that fraud prevention control thresholds and limits be set by reference to Fraud Risk Appetite, and the Fraud Risk Appetite itself must be formally defined, Board-endorsed, and monitored — creating a bidirectional dependency between prevention control calibration and appetite governance.

clause_a.excerpt: Member Organisations should define the approach to setting limits and thresholds for preventive controls (where applicable) in fraud prevention standards, considering: [...] 3. Fraud Risk Appetite.

clause_b.excerpt: The Fraud Risk Appetite of the Member Organisation should be defined to state the level of fraud risk the Member Organisation is willing to tolerate. [...] Fraud Risk Appetite should be reviewed on at least an annual basis and be formally endorsed by the Board.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_prevent||mark.implication: Prevention control thresholds (e.g., transaction limits, authentication step-up triggers) must be traceable to the documented Fraud Risk Appetite statement; any Board-approved appetite revision must trigger a review and update of corresponding preventive control parameters.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_detect||markd.why: The Detect domain is defined as the organisational capability whose primary operational expression is Fraud Detection Systems; the domain's standards mandate that Member Organisations define, implement, and maintain the systems and technology used to detect fraud, making Fraud Detection Systems the principal technical instrument of the Detect domain.

clause_a.excerpt: Fraud detection systems and controls are risk-based measures to identify fraud by looking for indicators in customer behaviours, transactional and non-transactional information. [...] Detective controls [...] typically [...] rely on technology to perform automated monitoring.

clause_b.excerpt: Fraud detection standards should include at a minimum: [...] 4. Systems and technology implemented to detect potential fraud (e.g., fraud detection software, alerts on high-value events or transactions, access monitoring, link analysis).

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_detect||markd.implication: Member Organisations must maintain documented fraud detection standards that specify each system or technology deployed, its data sources, calibration methodology, and rationale for adequacy relative to identified fraud risks — all subject to periodic effectiveness measurement and examiner review.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_respons.why: The Fraud Response Plan is the primary operative control within the Respond domain; the domain's introductory text explicitly mandates a 'robust Fraud Response Plan including clear procedures' as the mechanism for managing the organisational response, making the Plan a direct instantiation of the domain's requirements.

clause_a.excerpt: The Fraud Response Plan should be defined, approved, implemented and maintained and where appropriate aligned with the enterprise incident management process.

clause_b.excerpt: A timely and effective response to incidents of actual or suspected fraud is key to minimising losses and maximising the opportunity for recovery. Where fraud is suspected or detected, a robust Fraud Response Plan including clear procedures is required.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_respons.implication: A SAMA examiner will expect documented evidence that the Fraud Response Plan is formally approved, integrated with enterprise incident management, and subject to periodic effectiveness evaluation — not merely drafted but operationally embedded.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_detecti.why: The Framework explicitly requires that fraud detection standards be aligned to, and their focus determined by, the output of the Fraud Risk Assessment, making the Assessment the risk-based input that calibrates detection system design, thresholds, and scope.

clause_a.excerpt: The output of the Fraud Risk Assessment should be used to determine where detection activity is focused, and controls should be proportionate to the risk appetite of the organisation.

clause_b.excerpt: Member Organisations should conduct a Fraud Risk Assessment to identify fraud risks to which they or their customers are subject and assess the effectiveness of controls in place to mitigate the risks.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_detecti.implication: Detection system configuration (alert thresholds, monitored data sources, ML model scope) must be traceable to documented Fraud Risk Assessment outputs; any material change to the risk assessment must trigger a review and update of detection standards.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_risk_as.why: The Framework mandates a direct dependency: Fraud Risk Appetite must be based on the outcome of the Fraud Risk Assessment, and KRIs monitoring appetite exposure must reference risks identified in that same Assessment, creating a required evidence chain from risk identification to tolerance calibration.

clause_a.excerpt: The development of action plans to address residual risk that is outside of risk appetite.

clause_b.excerpt: The Member Organisation Fraud Risk Appetite should be based on the outcome of the Fraud Risk Assessment and aligned to the overall risk appetite of the organisation.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_risk_as.implication: Governance evidence must demonstrate a documented audit trail from Fraud Risk Assessment residual-risk outputs to Board-endorsed Fraud Risk Appetite thresholds, with KRI breach escalation procedures referencing specific appetite limits set through this cycle.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_detecti.why: Fraud Detection Systems explicitly feed outputs into the Intelligence Monitoring process: detected fraud typologies are listed as a mandatory minimum intelligence source, and Intelligence Monitoring findings must loop back to periodically recalibrate detection scenarios and parameters.

clause_a.excerpt: Systems and technology implemented to detect potential fraud (e.g., fraud detection software, alerts on high-value events or transactions, access monitoring, link analysis).

clause_b.excerpt: Periodically review scenarios and parameters to ensure they remain appropriate in view of the insights gathered in Intelligence Monitoring and/or the outcome of the Fraud Risk Assessment.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_fraud_detecti.implication: A RegTech architecture must implement a documented feedback loop where alert/detection outputs are ingested as structured intelligence inputs, and Intelligence Monitoring findings trigger scenario recalibration with an auditable change-log.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_intelligence_.why: The Counter-Fraud Department — which hosts or coordinates the Sectorial Anti-Fraud Committee function — is explicitly required to share Counter-Fraud Intelligence with SAMA and other sector organisations, directly linking the Intelligence Monitoring output to the inter-organisational committee mechanism.

clause_a.excerpt: Sharing relevant intelligence with internal and external stakeholders (e.g., Cyber, Business Operations or SAMA).

clause_b.excerpt: Sharing Counter-Fraud Intelligence with SAMA and other organisations in the sector.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_intelligence_.implication: Member Organisations must build an outbound intelligence-dissemination workflow — with defined classification, packaging, and dispatch controls — that can evidence timely sharing of fraud typologies and TTPs to SAMA and peer institutions via the sectorial committee channel.
markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_intelligence_.caveat: The source context does not render a discrete 'Sectorial Anti-Fraud Committee' article; the node is inferred from the Counter-Fraud Department's sector-sharing obligation. Locator for node B is therefore the Counter-Fraud Department control requirement rather than a standalone committee article.

markdown_sama_en_2217_ver1_due_diligence.why: SAMA_EN_2217 requires Customer Due Diligence to capture and validate customer identity to reduce external fraud losses, while SAMA_EN_4833 operationalises identity verification by mandating mobile-number matching via the national 'Absher/Taqqa' trusted source — directly implementing the verification step that fraud-focused CDD requires.

clause_a.excerpt: Member Organisations should establish controls to capture and validate the identity of customers to reduce the exposure to external fraud losses.

0.theme: This community covers the full AML/CTF compliance framework applicable to SAMA-supervised financial institutions, spanning the Anti-Money Laundering Law, the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing, and FATF standards. It clusters around the risk-based CDD lifecycle — from customer categorisation and risk assessment through enhanced/simplified due diligence, beneficial ownership, PEPs, and correspondent relationships — together with the governance, monitoring, reporting, and audit obligations that operationalise that lifecycle.
how_members_connect: Risk-Based Approach anchors the CDD tier selection (SDD/standard/EDD), with ML/TF Risk Assessment feeding account-type-specific controls for non-resident juristic persons, GCC non-bank companies, foreign investors, and liquidation accounts
The AML/CTF Guide implements the Anti-Money Laundering Law and CTF Law by translating statutory obligations into institutional procedures, citing FATF Recommendations as the international benchmark

KYC Principle and Beneficial Owner identification form the shared definitional spine that Due Diligence Measures, EDD, and Third-Party Reliance rules all reference, creating an obligation chain from customer onboarding through ongoing monitoring
Monitoring of Transactions and Activities and Reporting of Suspicious Transactions to SAFIU constitute the detection-and-disclosure control family, both citing the Anti-Money Laundering Law directly

Governance obligations (Board of Directors Responsibilities, Senior Management Responsibilities, AML/CTF Compliance Function, Independent Audit Function, Recruitment Criteria, Training) form a four-layer accountability structure that an examiner would trace from policy through to staff-level evidence

Wire Transfer and Correspondence Relationship rules extend CDD obligations to inter-institutional and cross-border payment chains, with Record Keeping requirements creating the evidence-retention layer across all nodes

1.theme: This community covers SAMA's prescriptive ruleset for the opening, operation, and closure of bank accounts across legally distinct customer categories — ranging from government entities and international organisations to civil society bodies and Hajj-related operators. The dominant regime is SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts, which imposes category-specific documentation, authorisation, and operational controls enforced through bank compliance and supported by inter-ministerial coordination.
how_members_connect: Rules for Bank Accounts is the primary instrument; all account-category rules (Government, Clearance, International Organisations, Endowments, Associations, Foundations, Cooperative Funds, Hajj/Pilgrim) reference SAMA as the supervisory authority and must conform to General Rules for Operation of Bank Accounts

Hajj Organizer and Pilgrim Affairs Office account rules are semantically paired and share identical structural controls — Dual Control/Joint Signature and Ministry of Hajj and Umrah authorisation — reflecting the elevated fiduciary and custody risk of pilgrim funds

Private Associations, Private Foundations, and Cooperative Associations/Funds all reference the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development for registration verification, creating a cross-ministerial documentary chain that Bank Compliance Departments must evidence

Disclosure and Enforcement on Accounts and Account Closure Rules define the lifecycle endpoints — attachment, freezing, and termination — within which all category-specific accounts must operate, with SAMA as the enforcement anchor
Cash and Deposit Controls (ATM/CAM) impose transaction-channel constraints applicable across account types, linking operational system capabilities to the same SAMA supervisory authority

Definitions and the General Rules nodes act as shared interpretive infrastructure, ensuring that category-specific rules inherit consistent terms for account holder, authorised signatory, and permissible operations

2.theme: This community covers SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework and its structured control domains (Govern, Prevent, Detect, Respond), which together define the enterprise-wide fraud risk management obligations for licensed financial institutions. It spans the fraud-specific regulatory instruments — including the POS Fraud Circular, Authentication Standard, and Tahaqaq identity verification service — alongside the Cyber Security Framework as a referenced dependency. The dominant regime is SAMA's counter-fraud supervisory mandate, measured through the Counter-Fraud Maturity Model.
how_members_connect: The Counter-Fraud Framework decomposes into four obligation domains (Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond), each referencing specific controls or sub-standards that institutions must implement and evidence.
The Governance Domain requires establishment of a Counter-Fraud Governance Committee (CFGC), creating a named accountability structure that an examiner would expect to see chartered and minuted.

The Prevent Domain consolidates upstream controls — Fraud Risk Assessment, Fraud Risk Appetite, Due Diligence Standards, Authentication Standard, and Intelligence Monitoring — forming a linked prevention control family.

Fraud Detection Systems (Detect Domain) draw inputs from both the Fraud Risk Assessment and Intelligence Monitoring, creating a data-flow obligation chain between risk quantification and real-time monitoring capabilities.
Intelligence Monitoring references the Sectorial Anti-Fraud Committee, establishing an inter-institutional information-sharing obligation and a SAMA-coordinated threat-intelligence channel.

The Preauthorization/Notification POS Fraud Circular and Tahaqaq Verification Service operationalise specific preventive controls within the Framework, anchoring abstract requirements to concrete transaction-level and identity-verification procedures.

3.theme: This community covers the AML/CTF compliance obligations imposed on Buy-Now-Pay-Later (BNPL) companies under SAMA's regulatory perimeter, sitting at the intersection of the Rules for Regulating BNPL Companies, the Finance Companies Control Law, the Anti-Money Laundering Law, and the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism. The central compliance problem is that BNPL companies, as SAMA-licensed finance entities, inherit the full AML/CTF obligation stack — including CDD, STR/FIU reporting, and preventive measures — while also carrying consumer credit and credit-bureau registration duties.
how_members_connect: The Rules for Regulating BNPL Companies bind BNPL Company to the Finance Companies Control Law, establishing the licensing basis that triggers SAMA supervisory authority and the AML/CTF compliance obligations.

BNPL Company's direct reference to AML/CTF Compliance Requirements creates the obligation chain into both the Anti-Money Laundering Law and the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism as the primary legislative sources.

The AML Law defines Predicate Offense, Due Diligence Measures, Confiscation, and the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence (GDFI) as the STR-receiving authority, forming the core ML control and enforcement vocabulary that BNPL firms must operationalise.

The CTF Law mirrors and extends AML obligations through Preventive Measures (CTF) and a separate GDFI (CTF) reporting channel, with the Permanent Committee for Combating Terrorism and its Financing providing the inter-agency enforcement layer; the shared_data_with edge between Preventive Measures (CTF) and Due Diligence Measures signals overlapping CDD obligations across both regimes.

Consumer Due Diligence Program (not 'Customer' CDD) reflects the BNPL-specific defined-term tension: BNPL rules use 'Consumer', while AML rules use 'Customer', requiring firms to map their onboarding workflow to satisfy both definitional scopes.

Credit Information Registration sits alongside AML/CTF obligations on the BNPL Company node, flagging a cross-regime data obligation where onboarding and CDD data feeds must also satisfy SIMAH/credit bureau reporting requirements.

4.theme: This community covers the SIFI resolution and recovery regime under KSA financial stability law, centering on the Competent Authority's powers (exercised by SAMA and/or CMA depending on the entity type) to plan for and execute orderly resolution of systemically important institutions. The cluster maps the full lifecycle from pre-failure recovery planning through triggered resolution procedures and post-resolution structural tools (Transitional Entity, Asset Management Entity, Sale), with CEDA involvement for decisions of systemic consequence.
how_members_connect: Competent Authority designation chain: SAMA and CMA are referenced as Competent Authority depending on the SIFI's regulated perimeter, creating a dual-regulator coordination obligation.

Pre-failure planning obligations: SIFIs (including those within a Financial Group) must maintain Board-approved Recovery Plans; the Competent Authority holds and reviews Resolution Plans, triggering an escalation path from recovery to resolution.

Resolution Procedures as an action menu: Amendment of Rights, Sale of the SIFI, Transitional Entity, and Asset Management Entity are enumerated tools available once Resolution Procedures are invoked, each with distinct asset/liability transfer implications.

Valuation dependency: Accredited Valuer is a precondition for exercising Resolution Procedures (particularly Sale and asset transfer tools), linking independent valuation to the legal validity of resolution actions.

Funding mechanism: Resolution Funds are referenced by the Competent Authority as a financing backstop for resolution execution, tying capital adequacy of the resolution fund to procedural feasibility.

Governance escalation: Resolution Plans require referral to the Council of Economic and Development Affairs for approval, embedding a sovereign-level decision gate above the Competent Authority for the most systemically sensitive actions.

5.theme: This community governs the licensed credit information ecosystem under the Credit Information Law and its Implementing Regulations, with SAMA as the licensing and supervisory authority. It defines the obligation chain among Credit Information Companies, their Members, and Consumers — covering data collection, record maintenance, consent, adverse-decision notification, and the formal dispute resolution pathway.
how_members_connect: Licensing as the entry gate: SAMA issues the Credit Information License; no entity may operate as a Credit Information Company or collect Credit Records without it, making the license the anchor control for the entire regime.

Membership Agreement as the B2B obligation instrument: Members (lenders, financiers) contract with Credit Information Companies via Membership Agreements that define data submission obligations and access rights, creating an enforceable B2B compliance layer.

Credit Record as the central data object: Negative Information populates the Credit Record; Negative Decisions are linked to it; Consumer Consent governs certain data-sharing uses — the record is the subject of all downstream obligations.

Consumer rights and consent chain: Consumer Consent is required for specific disclosures; Consumers have a right to access their Credit Record and invoke the Objection and Complaint Procedure if data is disputed or a Negative Decision is contested.

Dispute resolution escalation: The Objection and Complaint Procedure routes unresolved disputes to the Committee for Settlement of Credit Information Violations and Disputes, providing a statutory adjudication body outside ordinary courts.

Regulatory hierarchy: The Implementing Regulations of the Credit Information Law operationalize the Law's framework under SAMA's authority, creating a two-tier primary/secondary legislative structure that governs all member obligations.

6.theme: This community addresses the prudential and operational account-opening framework applicable to licensed payment companies in KSA, sitting at the intersection of the Payment Services Provider regime (capital adequacy, e-money classification, fund safeguarding) and SAMA's general bank account rules (KYC/AML, natural/juristic person onboarding, remote account opening). The cluster is the control surface for both licensing conditions and client-money protection obligations.
how_members_connect: Classification-driven capital obligations: Small Payment Company and E-Money Company classifications determine applicable Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements, making classification the first compliance trigger in the capital adequacy chain.

Safeguarding as a ring-fencing obligation: Protection and Safeguarding of Protected Funds is conceptually tied to E-Money classification and operationalized through Collection Accounts for Payment Companies' Clients — the account structure is the mechanism for client-money isolation.

KYC/AML as a cross-cutting precondition: General Instructions for Opening Bank Accounts and the Updating Account Data obligation both reference KYC Principle and AML/CFT Requirements, embedding CDD as a prerequisite for account opening and maintenance regardless of account type.

Account-opening rules as a tiered framework: Rules for Natural Persons, Juristic Persons, and Remote Opening each reference the General Instructions as the baseline, with Juristic Person rules additionally specifying purpose-specific accounts (crowdfunding collection, real estate escrow, payment company client accounts).

Purpose-specific collection accounts: Collection Accounts for Debt-Based Crowdfunding and Escrow Accounts for Real Estate Development appear under the Juristic Person rules, indicating that sector-specific licensing conditions (crowdfunding, real estate development) feed account-type obligations back into the payment account framework.

Ongoing capital as a dynamic prudential control: Ongoing Capital Requirements reference both classification tiers, requiring continuous monitoring rather than a one-time threshold check — implying a recurring capital adequacy reporting and breach-notification obligation.

7.theme: This community maps the intersection of the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) and the Credit Information Law as they apply to credit data processing by Credit Information Companies operating under SAMA supervision. It identifies where the PDPL's Controller/Processor/Data Subject framework overlays the credit-specific consent and record-handling obligations, creating a dual-regime compliance burden for entities processing credit data.
how_members_connect: Credit data as a PDPL-regulated personal data category: Credit Data Processing is explicitly referenced under the PDPL, treating credit records as personal data subject to PDPL obligations in addition to the Credit Information Law's sector-specific rules.

Dual supervisory authority: SAMA (Saudi Central Bank) is the sector regulator under the Credit Information Law; the Competent Authority (PDPL) (the SDAIA/NDMO framework) supervises PDPL compliance — Credit Information Companies face oversight from both, with potential for divergent enforcement.

Controller/Processor distinction applied to credit data flows: Credit Information Companies acting as data aggregators may be Controllers; member lenders submitting data may be joint Controllers or Processors depending on the arrangement — the PDPL's definitional framework must be mapped onto the Membership Agreement structure.

Data Subject rights as an overlay on Consumer rights: PDPL Data Subject rights (access, correction, erasure) run alongside the Credit Information Law's Consumer objection and consent rights — entities must satisfy both regimes when a Consumer/Data Subject challenges their Credit Record.

Credit Information Law as lex specialis: The PDPL references the Credit Information Law as a domain-specific instrument, suggesting the Credit Information Law's consent and disclosure rules are the primary standard for credit data, with the PDPL filling residual gaps.

SAMA's dual role: SAMA (Saudi Central Bank) appears both as the Credit Information Law regulator and as a Saudi Central Bank (PDPL) reference node, indicating SAMA's internal data processing activities are themselves subject to PDPL obligations.

8.theme: This community covers the fraud prevention and detection control framework applicable to licensed banks under SAMA supervision, anchored by the Financial Fraud Combating Guide and supported by the Banking Control Law and payment-channel-specific obligations. It sits at the intersection of prudential licensing, operational fraud governance, and point-of-sale CDD requirements, creating an obligation chain from institutional licensing through to channel-level controls.
how_members_connect: The Financial Fraud Combating Guide operationalises fraud obligations that derive authority from the Banking Control Law and cross-reference the AML Law, binding all licensed banks as defined under that Law.

The Financial Fraud Combating Unit is the designated internal governance structure mandated by the Guide, with its charter and responsibilities shaped by the Governance and Responsibilities framework within the same instrument.

The POS KYC Verification Circular extends fraud-related CDD obligations to the point-of-sale channel, referencing both the Banking Control Law and Payment Service Providers Regulatory Rules, linking merchant-facing controls to the broader fraud regime.

SAMA as Monetary Authority exercises licensing authority under the Banking Control Law and supervises compliance with both the fraud guide and the POS circular, creating a single supervisory principal across these instruments.
Banking Licensing Provisions establish the threshold condition (licensed bank status) that determines which entities fall within scope of the fraud guide and POS verification requirements.

9.theme: This community covers the AML/CFT/PF risk assessment and beneficial ownership identification regime as it applies across banks and payment service providers in KSA, spanning primary law, implementing regulations, and SAMA circulars targeting specific high-risk customer categories. The cluster is defined by the obligation to identify, verify, and document beneficial owners using prescribed methods including the Waatheq platform, with payment regulation layered as a parallel licensing regime sharing implementation rule cross-references.
how_members_connect: The Implementing Regulation to the AML Law and the Implementing Regulations of the Law on Combating Terrorist Crimes and its Financing jointly define the CDD and beneficial ownership standards that the Waatheq, NPO, and Awqaf circulars operationalise for specific entity types.

The three beneficial owner circulars (Waatheq, NPOs, Awqaf) each reference the AML Implementing Regulation directly, creating a tiered obligation structure: primary law → implementing regulation → sector/entity-specific circular.

The Business Risk Assessment Guide (AML/CFT/PF) references both AML and CTF implementing regulations, positioning enterprise-level risk assessment as the upstream control that must account for the entity-specific beneficial ownership obligations below it.

The Implementing Regulation to the Law of Payments and Payment Services references the Implementation Rules for Banking Control Law, establishing that payment service providers inherit AML-aligned implementation expectations in addition to their payment-specific licensing conditions.

The Law of Payments and Payment Services sits as the primary authority for the payments regime, with its implementing regulation creating a parallel but cross-referenced track to banking AML rules, relevant when assessing PSP customer due diligence obligations.

10.theme: This community covers the licensing, prudential, and product-specific regulatory framework for finance companies and BNPL operators in KSA, anchored by the Finance Companies Control Law and its implementing regulations, with the Companies Law and Capital Market Law providing foundational corporate and securities law references. The BNPL-specific instruments (cap circular and regulation rules) represent the product-level overlay that compliance and RegTech controls must map against the parent licensing regime.
how_members_connect: The Implementing Regulations of Finance Companies Control Law operationalise the primary Law, referencing both the Capital Market Law and Companies Law as the corporate governance and securities framework within which licensed finance companies must operate.

The Finance Companies Control Law (English Translation) similarly cross-references Capital Market Law and Companies Law, confirming that finance company licensing conditions are calibrated against broader KSA corporate and capital markets requirements.
The BNPL Companies Regulation Rules establish the dedicated product regime for BNPL operators, sitting as a subordinate instrument beneath the Finance Companies Control Law framework.

The BNPL Financing Cap Increase Circular amends or elaborates the financing exposure limits within the BNPL Rules, referencing the Implementing Regulations directly — creating a three-tier obligation chain (Law → Implementing Regulations → Circular) for cap compliance monitoring.

The cluster defines the scope boundary for 'Consumer' under the BNPL regime, distinct from AML 'Customer' definitions, which is a critical cross-regime distinction for CDD workflow design in BNPL platforms.

11.theme: This community covers the Targeted Financial Sanctions (TFS) compliance regime in KSA, comprising two parallel TFS rule instruments, the primary AML and CTF laws, and the AML/CTF operational and risk assessment guides. It represents the sanctions screening and freeze-without-delay obligation cluster, where regulatory controls must address both UN-listed and domestically designated persons across all regulated entity types.
how_members_connect: TFS Rules 10667 and 10668 are semantically parallel instruments, each referencing the Anti-Money Laundering Law and Counter-Terrorism Crimes and Financing Law as their dual legal bases, establishing that TFS obligations derive from both regimes simultaneously.

Both TFS rule instruments reference the AML/CTF Guide, positioning the Guide as the operational implementation reference for screening procedures, freeze obligations, and reporting requirements mandated by the TFS Rules.

The AML/CTF/CPF Business Risk Assessment Guide references the AML Law, CTF Law, and the AML/CTF Guide, anchoring TFS risk as a component of enterprise-level AML/CTF/PF risk assessment rather than a standalone process.

The Anti-Money Laundering Law and Counter-Terrorism Crimes and Financing Law function as the shared primary law layer, with TFS rules and guides acting as subordinate instruments that must be read consistently with both statutes.

The cluster implies a screening and monitoring control family: real-time or pre-transaction name screening against consolidated sanctions lists, freeze execution workflows, reporting to competent authorities, and documented risk assessment of TFS exposure by business line.

12.theme: This community covers the consumer-facing obligations imposed on payment service licensees under SAMA's Payment Services regulatory regime: execution integrity, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, refund entitlements, and dispute resolution. It maps the obligation chain from correct payment order execution through to consumer redress, forming the core of payment consumer-protection compliance.
how_members_connect: Payment Order Execution Rules set the baseline for what constitutes correct execution, which directly triggers liability analysis under Unauthorized Payment Liability when execution fails or fraud occurs

Unauthorized Payment Liability and Refund Rights for Payment Transactions are causally linked — a finding of unauthorized payment activates the refund entitlement and defines who bears the loss (licensee vs. payer)
Complaints and Disputes references Unauthorized Payment Liability, establishing the procedural channel through which consumers assert execution failures and liability claims
Account Information and Payment Initiation Services references Payment Order Execution Rules, extending execution-quality and liability obligations to AISP/PISP actors operating on behalf of payers

Licensee Change Notification Obligations references Payment Order Execution Rules, indicating that material changes to service terms or infrastructure must be disclosed in a way that preserves execution continuity and consumer awareness

Collectively these nodes define the auditable evidence trail an examiner expects: timestamped execution records, unauthorized-transaction dispute logs, refund processing timelines, and consumer notification records

13.theme: This community governs the licensing, account-lifecycle management, and electronic record infrastructure for payment service providers and prepaid instrument issuers under SAMA's PSP and Prepaid Payment Services frameworks. It links market-entry authorization conditions to ongoing operational controls over account states and record integrity.
how_members_connect: Payment Service Provider Licensing Requirements and Regulatory Rules for Prepaid Payment Services are conceptually co-dependent: prepaid issuers must satisfy PSP licensing conditions as a prerequisite, making licensing the gateway control for prepaid operations
Electronic Record Requirements supports both licensing and account-management obligations by defining the retention and integrity standards that evidence compliance across the account lifecycle
Freezing of Bank Accounts references Electronic Record Requirements, indicating that account-freeze actions must be documented in the mandated electronic record format to be valid and auditable

Inoperative Accounts references both Freezing of Bank Accounts and Regulatory Rules for Prepaid Payment Services, creating a state-transition chain: inactive status can trigger freeze procedures, with specific prepaid-service rules governing dormancy treatment

An examiner would expect system controls demonstrating: license-status checks at onboarding, automated dormancy/freeze state transitions with audit logs, and retention of electronic records meeting SAMA-specified standards

14.theme: This community consolidates SAMA's counter-fraud mandatory requirements across both banks and finance companies, anchored by the Counter-Fraud Framework (CFF) as the governing standard and implemented through binding circulars. It forms the control-family backbone for fraud risk management obligations applicable to licensed financial institutions.
how_members_connect: Counter-Fraud Framework (CFF) is the primary normative document; Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements (10530) references it directly, establishing the CFF as the interpretive authority for specific fraud controls

Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements Circular (10529) and its substantive counterpart (10530) are semantically paired — the circular is the transmittal instrument and (10530) contains the enforceable requirements text

Both circulars (10529 and 10530) reference Anti-Fraud Rules for Finance Companies (circular 381000103246), extending counter-fraud obligations explicitly into the finance company regime and flagging a cross-entity-type compliance perimeter

The cluster implies a unified control family: fraud detection and prevention programs, incident reporting obligations, staff awareness requirements, and governance accountability — applicable to both banks and finance companies with sector-specific calibration

An examiner would expect evidence of CFF-aligned fraud risk assessments, documented controls mapped to the fundamental requirements, and proof that finance companies have implemented the sector-specific circular obligations

15.theme: This community addresses the classification, oversight principles, and disclosure standards for systemically important payment and settlement infrastructures in Saudi Arabia, sitting at the intersection of SAMA's domestic Important Payment Systems regime and international CPMI-IOSCO standards. It defines the regulatory expectations for financial market infrastructure (FMI) operators regarding resilience, settlement finality, and public accountability.
how_members_connect: Important Payment Systems Classification is the gateway node: designation as an important payment system triggers application of the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMIs) as the governing prudential standard

Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures cites the CPMI-IOSCO Disclosure Framework, linking substantive FMI requirements to the structured self-assessment and public disclosure obligations that demonstrate PFMI compliance

Settlement Finality and Insolvency references Important Payment Systems Classification, indicating that finality protections — shielding settled transactions from insolvency reversal — apply specifically within classified systems, a critical legal-certainty control

CPMI-IOSCO Disclosure Framework functions as an accountability and transparency mechanism, requiring classified FMIs to publish standardized assessments against the PFMIs — auditable by SAMA and market participants

An examiner would expect: documented classification analysis, PFMI self-assessments mapped to each applicable principle, legal opinions confirming settlement finality under KSA insolvency law, and published CPMI-IOSCO disclosure reports

16.theme: Systemically Important Financial Institution (SIFI) designation and enhanced prudential obligations under KSA law. This community covers the primary legislative framework and its implementing regulations governing identification, requirements, and supervisory expectations for institutions whose failure could threaten financial stability. The cluster is tight because the Implementing Regulations derive directly from and operationalise the Law, forming a two-tier primary/secondary instrument pair.
how_members_connect: The Implementing Regulations reference the SIFI Law as their legal basis, creating a direct parent-child instrument relationship
Designation criteria, thresholds, and methodology flow from the Law into the Implementing Regulations as enforceable detail
Enhanced capital, liquidity, recovery, and resolution requirements are anchored in the Law and specified in the Implementing Regulations
Supervisory powers and SAMA intervention triggers are established in the Law and procedurally elaborated in the Implementing Regulations
Compliance obligations (reporting, governance, systemic risk buffers) are traceable through both instruments as a single control chain

17.theme: Consumer-facing disclosure and contractual transparency obligations under SAMA's customer protection and payments regulatory perimeter. This community covers the pre-contractual and contractual information requirements that regulated entities must satisfy, linking general protection principles to specific framework contract disclosure rules relevant to payment services and consumer finance. The cluster reflects the obligation chain from high-level principles to operationally specific document requirements.
how_members_connect: Framework Contract Information Requirements reference Customer Protection Principles as the normative foundation for disclosure obligations
Both instruments share the defined term 'Customer' and apply to retail-facing regulated entities
Disclosure timing, format, and content obligations in the Framework Contract rules operationalise the fairness and transparency principles
Pre-contractual information duties create a document-production and evidence-retention requirement auditable against both instruments
Cross-regime interaction: 'Consumer' definitions may diverge when AML CDD obligations apply to the same customer relationship

18.theme: SAMA's statutory supervisory and enforcement authority over licensed financial institutions in the KSA. This community covers the legal basis, scope of powers, and procedural framework through which SAMA conducts examinations, issues directives, and imposes sanctions. It is the foundational governance cluster underpinning all other regulatory regimes, as every sector-specific rule ultimately derives enforceability from SAMA's supervisory mandate.
how_members_connect: Supervision and Enforcement instruments reference SAMA as the competent authority, grounding all powers in SAMA's enabling legislation
Examination, investigation, and sanction procedures are defined here and cross-referenced by sector-specific frameworks (AML, payments, consumer finance)
Licensing conditions and ongoing compliance obligations across regimes are enforceable through the mechanisms established in this cluster
Reporting and notification obligations to SAMA in other regimes are backed by enforcement consequences articulated here
Auditors and examiners use this cluster to establish the legal basis for findings, directives, and remediation timelines

19.theme: Consumer finance debt portfolio transactions intersecting with domestic payment infrastructure, specifically the SARIE Fast Transfer System. This community covers the regulatory conditions governing the purchase of consumer finance receivables and the settlement or notification mechanics that reference SARIE, linking credit/finance company obligations to payment system operational requirements. The cluster highlights a cross-regime interaction between consumer finance rules and payment infrastructure compliance.
how_members_connect: Consumer Finance Debt Purchase Instructions reference SARIE Fast Transfer System for settlement or disbursement mechanics associated with purchased receivables
Debt purchase eligibility, pricing, and borrower notification obligations in the Instructions interact with real-time payment capabilities of SARIE
Borrower rights on debt transfer (notification, continuity of terms) create data and messaging requirements executable via SARIE infrastructure
Finance company licensing conditions span both instruments: credit origination rules and payment system access/participation rules
Operational risk and settlement finality considerations under SARIE are relevant to the timing obligations imposed by the Debt Purchase Instructions

20.theme: This community covers the governance and transparency obligation requiring regulated entities to maintain a register of controllers — persons or entities with significant ownership or influence. It sits at the intersection of SAMA licensing/authorisation conditions and AML/CTF beneficial-ownership frameworks, ensuring supervisory visibility into control structures.
how_members_connect: Controller identification links directly to UBO determination obligations under AML/CTF rules
Register maintenance is a licensing condition auditable by SAMA examiners at authorisation and ongoing supervision stages
Data held in the register feeds CDD/KYB workflows when the regulated entity itself is onboarded by another obliged party
Changes in control typically trigger prior-approval or notification obligations to SAMA
Register accuracy underpins fit-and-proper assessments for significant shareholders and senior managers

21.theme: This community addresses SAMA's policy framework for broadening access to regulated financial products and services among underserved segments. It intersects consumer-protection, payments/PSP licensing, and BNPL/finance-company regimes by setting design principles that obliged entities must embed in product development and delivery strategies.
how_members_connect: Inclusion principles constrain product eligibility criteria, preventing blanket exclusions that conflict with SAMA access mandates
Simplified or tiered CDD requirements for low-risk segments are a direct RegTech implication of inclusion policy
PSP and BNPL licensing conditions may reference inclusion commitments as part of authorisation or business-plan approval
Affordability and suitability assessments under consumer-protection rules operationalise inclusion at the product level
Reporting obligations may require entities to evidence outreach metrics to underserved demographics for SAMA review

22.name: Limited Network Provider Registration
22.theme: This community covers the registration regime applicable to Limited Network Service Providers (LNSPs) — entities issuing payment instruments usable only within a restricted network or for a limited range of goods and services. It sits within the payments regulatory perimeter, defining the lighter-touch authorisation pathway that is nonetheless subject to SAMA oversight and defined scope conditions.
how_members_connect: Registration scope conditions (network/product limits) determine whether an entity falls inside or outside full PSP licensing requirements
Breach of network or value thresholds triggers reclassification and potential full-licence obligation
AML/CTF applicability is modulated by LNSP status — exemption conditions must be actively monitored and documented
SAMA registration records must be maintained as evidence of authorised status for counterparty due-diligence purposes
Consumer-protection obligations attach proportionally; entities must evidence which rules apply given their registered scope
Ongoing compliance requires monitoring of instrument usage to confirm continued eligibility for the limited-network carve-out

23.theme: This community governs the requirement for regulated entities — particularly payment service providers, finance companies, and intermediaries — to hold Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII) as a condition of authorisation or ongoing licence maintenance. It is a financial-resilience and consumer-redress control sitting within SAMA's prudential and licensing frameworks.
how_members_connect: PII adequacy is a licensing condition; SAMA examiners expect documented evidence of current, sufficient cover at authorisation and renewal
Minimum coverage thresholds and policy terms must align with the regulated activity type and transaction volumes
PII interacts with capital-adequacy requirements as a complementary loss-absorption mechanism for operational and liability risks
Consumer-protection rules rely on PII as a backstop for client redress where entity assets are insufficient
Lapse or material change in PII coverage constitutes a notifiable event requiring prompt disclosure to SAMA
Outsourcing and third-party arrangements may affect PII scope; entities must ensure cover extends to relevant operational risks
